description: Agent Card builder-level wire-shape parity (Algorithm A-CARD). The runner builds an AgentCard via AgentCardBuilder.build(registry, name, description, version, url, capabilities, security_schemes) where `security_schemes` is the FLAT descriptor returned by JWTAuthenticator.security_schemes(), serializes to the A2A 1.0 JSON wire form (camelCase), and partial-matches expected_card. Locks the proto3 securitySchemes oneof shape, supportedInterfaces (no top-level url), the public-card skill-visibility filter (srs FR-AGC-003) and the apcore: annotation tags (srs FR-SKL-004). NOTE: agent name/version fallback and capabilities.{streaming,pushNotifications} computation live in the serve() layer (not the builder) and are covered by per-SDK TC-AGC unit tests, not by this fixture.

test_cases.description: The flat {type:http,scheme:bearer,bearerFormat:JWT} descriptor is transformed into the A2A 1.0 proto3 oneof shape on the wire (scheme type = the oneof key httpAuthSecurityScheme, NOT a `type` field).

apcore behavioral annotations reach the wire as namespaced entries in the standard `tags` field, in the fixed order readonly, destructive, idempotent, requires-approval, appended after the module's own tags (srs FR-SKL-004). A2A 1.0 AgentSkill has no extensions or metadata member, so tags is the only carrier.

Only true flags are emitted; false, absent, and a descriptor with no annotations object at all all produce no tag. Absence means "not asserted", never "asserted false" — matching how the apcore MCP binding maps the same annotations onto optional hints.

A module annotated requires_approval is absent from the PUBLIC card even with no ACL configured (srs FR-AGC-003 criterion 7). It reappears on the extended card, which is what gives capabilities.extendedAgentCard something to mean.

A skill the ACL denies to the anonymous principal (@external) is absent from the public card (srs FR-AGC-003 criterion 6). Before this rule Python and TypeScript advertised every registered skill — id, name, description and full input schema — to any anonymous caller, because /.well-known/ is auth-exempt by design.

The extended card carries what the AUTHENTICATED caller may invoke, including requires_approval skills (srs FR-AGC-004). Python previously returned CopyFrom(base_card) — a verbatim copy — while Rust and TypeScript did not route the endpoint at all despite all three advertising capabilities.extendedAgentCard.

A skill the ACL ALLOWS the anonymous principal but gates behind a human (approval: required, apcore >= 0.28.0 PROTOCOL_SPEC §6.1.6) is absent from the public card, on the same terms as an annotated one (srs FR-AGC-003 criterion 11). The annotation and the ACL rule are the two sources apcore §6.9 composes by union; a binding that reads only the annotation leaves this skill advertised to callers who cannot just call it.

The same ACL-gated skill is PRESENT on the extended card: the caller is authorized and the gate is a prompt they can satisfy, not a refusal (srs FR-AGC-004 criteria 2 and 10). This is the case that separates the two accessors — apcore's legacy boolean ACL.check folds authorization and approval together and returns false here, so a binding filtering on it would delete the skill from BOTH cards and report a refusal the ACL never issued. Filtering on ACL.check_access / checkAccess and reading only `access` is the contract.

apcore's reserved management namespace (system.*, PROTOCOL_SPEC §6.7) is absent from the public card with NO ACL configured (srs FR-AGC-003 criteria 12 and 13). This is the case both ACL-shaped models leave open: the ACL predicates are empty, and the requires_approval annotation covers only system.control.*, so the six read modules — which enumerate the deployment's module inventory, health and usage — would otherwise be published by id, name, description and full input schema to any anonymous caller on the auth-exempt /.well-known/ route. A binding must not read `no ACL` as `advertise everything`.

The same system.* skills ARE on the extended card, filtered per identity like any other skill (srs FR-AGC-004 criterion 11). The namespace exclusion is a property of the public card, not of the skill: an authenticated management agent the ACL permits must still be able to discover the surface it is entitled to drive. system.control.update_config is present because requires_approval keeps a skill on the extended card (criterion 2), so this case also proves the two rules compose rather than one masking the other.

known_divergences: auth.md once wrongly showed securityRequirements as [{"bearerAuth":[]}]; the locked value is always empty. On the JSON wire (proto3) an empty repeated/map field is omitted, so the runner treats an absent securitySchemes/securityRequirements as empty rather than asserting a literal [] / {}.
TS/Rust previously emitted the flat security-scheme descriptor on the wire; fixed via toA2ASecurityScheme / to_a2a_security_schemes so all three now emit the oneof shape asserted here.
provider may be null or an object depending on configuration; not asserted here.

Skill visibility converged 2026-08-26 (srs FR-AGC-003 / FR-AGC-004). Before this fixture the three bindings gave three different answers to "which skills does an unauthenticated caller see": Rust filtered the public card per caller (server/handlers.rs acl_filtered_card + FilteredCard), Python and TypeScript filtered nothing at all (_build_skills / buildSkills iterate registry.list() and never consult the ACL). None matched the static two-tier split the spec described. Breaking change for Python and TypeScript deployments that relied on the public card as a full catalogue.

apcore 0.28.0 (PROTOCOL_SPEC §6.1.6) split one ACL verdict into two independent axes — authorization and approval — and made the legacy boolean ACL.check fail closed on an approval requirement. All three bindings filtered cards on that boolean, so an allow-with-approval skill would have silently vanished from the extended card too. Fixed 2026-09-01 by moving every card filter to the structured accessor (check_access / checkAccess); the two acl_approval_gated cases pin both directions.

apcore-a2a#5: `sys_modules` / `sysModules` was a no-op in all three bindings — Python and TypeScript built the registration Config as `{apcore: {sys_modules: {enabled}}}` while apcore reads `sys_modules.enabled` in legacy mode, and Rust passed `Config::default()` outright and discarded the Result. So no `system.*` module ever reached a card, and the exposure the two `system_namespace` cases pin was latent rather than live. Fixed 2026-09-01 together with the namespace rule, deliberately in that order: repairing the config path alone is what would have opened the hole.

Cases carrying `card_variant`, `acl_rules` or `identity` exercise the serve()/factory layer rather than AgentCardBuilder.build() alone, since the anonymous-principal filter needs the executor's ACL. Runners that only drive the builder skip them; the per-SDK card-visibility tests cover the same assertions.
